options: It gave women the right to vote in colonial elections for the first time
It limited voting to men who owned a certain amount of property
It made voting compulsory for every adult man in the two colonies
Voters could choose freely without employers or landlords watching
questions.explanation: Before the secret ballot men voted publicly, so bosses, landlords and others could pressure or punish them. A printed ballot marked in private removed that pressure, and Britain copied it in 1872. Women first won the vote in South Australia in 1894, and compulsory federal voting came in 1924.

questions.stem: In 1897 Catherine Helen Spence became Australia's first female political candidate. What was she standing for?
options: A seat in the Senate at the first federal election in March 1901
The office of Lord Mayor of the city of Adelaide
A seat in the British House of Commons in London
Election to the Federal Convention drafting the Constitution
questions.explanation: Spence, a South Australian writer and reformer, stood as one of the colony's delegates to the 1897 Federal Convention. She was not elected, but her campaign showed women entering politics before Federation. She also campaigned for proportional representation, which the Senate later adopted.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave most adult women the right to vote and stand in federal elections. Which group did it specifically exclude?
options: Most Aboriginal people and people of Asian, African or Pacific Island origin
Women who were not married or who did not own property of their own
Anyone born outside Australia, including migrants who had come out from Britain
Men who had not served in a colonial army or naval force
questions.explanation: The Act barred 'aboriginal natives' of Australia, Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands (except New Zealand) unless they already had a state vote. It gave the vote to women whether married or not, and British-born residents could vote. All Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people did not gain the federal vote until 1962.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth began paying old-age pensions in 1909 and a maternity allowance in 1912. Why are these reforms linked to the idea of Australia as a 'social laboratory'?
options: The new nation used laws to guarantee people a decent standard of living
Britain paid for them to reward Australia's loyalty to the Empire
They were paid only to returned soldiers and their families
They were copied from schemes already running in every other Western country
questions.explanation: Early Commonwealth governments experimented with laws such as pensions, the maternity allowance and arbitrated wages to protect ordinary people, which drew attention overseas. Only a few places, such as Germany and New Zealand, had pensions earlier, so they were not copied from everywhere. The benefits also excluded many Aboriginal and Asian Australians, which shows whose welfare the reforms protected.

questions.stem: After the defeat of the great maritime and shearers' strikes of 1890–91, many unionists turned to politics. What happened next?
options: A federal law made all strikes in Australia illegal
Labor candidates won many seats in the 1891 NSW election
Trade unions were banned throughout the Australian colonies
Shearers founded Australia's first Communist Party
questions.explanation: Unionists concluded they needed their own representatives in Parliament, and Labor Electoral League candidates won 35 seats in New South Wales in 1891. Unions were not banned, though strike leaders such as some Queensland shearers were jailed. The Communist Party of Australia was founded much later, in 1920, and there was no federal Parliament until 1901.

questions.stem: Soon after World War I began, the War Precautions Act 1914 gave the Commonwealth government sweeping powers. Which was one of them?
options: Censoring newspapers and letters
Conscripting men to fight overseas
Taking ownership of all farmland
Giving women the vote for the war
questions.explanation: The Act allowed censorship, internment of 'enemy aliens' and rule by regulation for the duration of the war. Conscription for overseas service is the tempting answer, but it was never introduced in World War I: voters rejected it in 1916 and 1917. Women already had the federal vote from 1902.

questions.stem: Australians voted on conscription for overseas service in 1916 and 1917. Why are these votes described as plebiscites rather than referendums?
options: They asked for voters' opinion and could not change the Constitution
Only men of military age were allowed to take part in them
They were held in each state on a different day of the year
Their results could be overruled by a ruling of the High Court of Australia
questions.explanation: A referendum is the vote required to change the Constitution, while a plebiscite simply asks the people's view on a question; the government was not legally bound by the result. All voters on the rolls, including women, could vote. Both conscription proposals were narrowly defeated, deeply dividing the nation.

questions.stem: Painters of the Heidelberg School, such as Tom Roberts, Frederick McCubbin and Arthur Streeton, are linked with nationalism around Federation because they:
options: drew cartoons attacking Federation for The Bulletin
painted Australian light, landscapes and bush work
copied English country scenes from imported prints
painted murals for Parliament House in Canberra
questions.explanation: Works such as Shearing the Rams and The Pioneer celebrated the bush, rural labour and the Australian landscape, helping shape a sense of national identity in the 1880s and 1890s. Copying English scenes is exactly what they moved away from. Parliament House in Canberra did not open until 1927, and The Bulletin was a champion of Australian nationalism rather than an enemy of it.

questions.stem: The American colonists' slogan 'No taxation without representation' objected to:
options: French taxes charged on goods traded through Canada
the Church of England collecting tithes in the colonies
being taxed by a British Parliament they could not elect
paying taxes set by their own elected colonial assemblies
questions.explanation: The colonists had no members in the Parliament at Westminster, so they argued that Parliament had no right to tax them through measures such as the Stamp Act and the tea duty. Taxes passed by their own assemblies were exactly what they accepted. Protests such as the Boston Tea Party in 1773 grew out of this principle.

questions.stem: Which document, adopted on 4 July 1776, announced that the thirteen American colonies were no longer ruled by Britain?
options: The Bill of Rights
The Treaty of Paris
The Declaration of Independence
The United States Constitution
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence, mainly drafted by Thomas Jefferson, claimed that all men are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. The Constitution (1787) and Bill of Rights (1791) came later and set up the new government. The Treaty of Paris in 1783 was when Britain finally recognised American independence.

questions.stem: The storming of the Bastille in Paris on 14 July 1789 is seen as the start of the French Revolution because:
options: the members of the Estates-General had been locked in it
crowds seized a royal fortress that symbolised the king's power
it was the place where King Louis XVI was later executed by guillotine
Napoleon used it as the setting to crown himself emperor
questions.explanation: The Bastille was a fortress-prison, and its capture showed that ordinary Parisians would use force against royal authority; 14 July is still France's national day. Louis XVI was guillotined in a public square in 1793, not at the Bastille, which had been demolished. Napoleon crowned himself in Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1804.

questions.stem: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) is seen as a foundation of modern human rights because it stated that:
options: all property should be owned in common and shared out by the state
women and men must have exactly the same rights to vote and hold office
men are born free and equal in rights, and power comes from the nation
kings rule by divine right with the blessing of the Catholic Church
questions.explanation: The Declaration rejected rule by divine right and set out rights such as liberty, property, equality before the law and free expression. It did not grant women equal political rights — Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791 to protest that. Shared ownership of all property was a later socialist idea.

questions.stem: During the Reign of Terror in France (1793–94):
options: thousands of suspected enemies of the Revolution were executed
Napoleon's armies invaded Russia and were forced to retreat
the king restored absolute monarchy and closed the National Assembly
British troops occupied Paris and returned the king to power
questions.explanation: Led by Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, the revolutionary government sent thousands to the guillotine as traitors, before Robespierre himself was executed in 1794. The invasion of Russia happened in 1812 under Napoleon, who rose to power after the Terror. Louis XVI had already been executed in January 1793.

questions.stem: Otto von Bismarck is remembered for:
options: founding the League of Nations after World War I
uniting the German states into an empire in 1871
leading the Redshirts in the unification of Italy
overthrowing the Russian tsar during the war of 1917
questions.explanation: As Prussia's chief minister, Bismarck used wars against Denmark, Austria and France to bring the German states together, and the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871. Leading the Redshirts describes Giuseppe Garibaldi, whose campaigns helped create the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Both unifications show the rise of nation-states in the 1800s.

questions.stem: US President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918) included the principle of 'self-determination'. What did it mean?
options: Each country should pay for all of its own war damage itself
Germany should be divided into four occupation zones
Colonies should be shared out among the victors
Peoples should be able to choose their own government
questions.explanation: Self-determination meant national groups, such as Poles and Czechs, should form their own states, and new nations were created from the old empires after 1918. Dividing Germany into four zones happened after World War II, in 1945. In practice German colonies were handed to the victors as 'mandates', which is why the colonies option describes what happened rather than what Wilson's principle said.

questions.stem: At the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, Australia's Prime Minister Billy Hughes argued strongly for:
options: control of German New Guinea and protection for White Australia
Japan's racial equality clause to be added to the League Covenant
Australia to leave the British Empire and become a republic
Germany to pay no reparations at all for the cost of the war
questions.explanation: Hughes won Australia a mandate over German New Guinea and fought to protect the White Australia policy. He strongly opposed Japan's proposed racial equality clause, fearing it would threaten immigration restrictions, so supporting it is the reverse of his position. He also wanted Germany to pay heavy reparations.

questions.stem: Which was a major weakness of the League of Nations, set up after World War I?
options: The United States never joined it
Only European nations could become members
Germany was a founding permanent member
It met only once every ten years
questions.explanation: Although Wilson proposed the League, the US Senate refused to join, so it lacked the world's most powerful country. The League also had no army of its own and its Council needed unanimous decisions. Countries outside Europe, including Australia and Japan, were members, and Germany was not admitted until 1926.

questions.stem: In late 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power in Russia. Who led them?
options: Vladimir Lenin
Joseph Stalin
Tsar Nicholas II
Alexander Kerensky
questions.explanation: Lenin led the Bolshevik revolution and the new communist state until his death in 1924, when Stalin rose to power. Kerensky headed the Provisional Government that the Bolsheviks overthrew, and Tsar Nicholas II had already abdicated earlier in 1917. The revolution made communism a powerful ideology in the interwar years.

questions.stem: Who led the Fascists to power in Italy in 1922?
options: Francisco Franco
Benito Mussolini
Adolf Hitler
Giuseppe Garibaldi
questions.explanation: Mussolini became Prime Minister after the March on Rome in 1922 and turned Italy into a one-party fascist state. Hitler came to power in Germany later, in 1933, and Franco won the Spanish Civil War in 1939. Garibaldi was a nineteenth-century hero of Italian unification.

questions.stem: Why did fascist and Nazi parties win growing support in Italy and Germany between the wars?
options: Long traditions of stable democracy that most voters wanted to protect
Pressure from the League of Nations for stronger national leaders
Economic crisis, anger at the peace settlement and fear of communism
Strong economic growth through the 1920s and the early 1930s
questions.explanation: Unemployment and hardship, especially after the Great Depression, resentment of the post-war treaties, and fear of a communist revolution led many people to support strong leaders who promised order and national pride. Both countries had weak and fairly new democracies, and the Depression brought economic collapse rather than growth.

questions.stem: What did James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (about 1764) allow a worker to do?
options: Weave cloth on a loom driven by steam power
Pull the seeds out of raw cotton very quickly
Print coloured patterns onto finished cloth
Spin several threads at once instead of one
questions.explanation: The jenny let one spinner work several spindles at once, at first eight, greatly increasing thread production in cottage industry. Power weaving came with Edmund Cartwright's power loom in 1785, and the cotton gin that removed seeds was invented by Eli Whitney in the United States in 1793.

questions.stem: Richard Arkwright's mill at Cromford (1771) is often called one of the first modern factories because:
options: water-powered machines and workers were gathered in one building on shifts
workers spun cotton at home and brought the thread to the mill for sale
it was the first workplace in Britain to be lit and powered entirely by electricity
it was owned and run by the British government to supply the navy
questions.explanation: Arkwright's water frame needed a river for power, so he brought machines and workers together under one roof, working long shifts set by the clock. Spinning at home describes the older domestic or 'putting-out' system that factories replaced. Electricity did not power factories until the late 1800s.

questions.stem: James Watt's improvements to the steam engine from the 1760s mattered because they:
options: made engines far more efficient and able to drive factory machines
produced the very first engine of any kind for pumping water out of mines
allowed engines to run on electricity instead of coal and water
created the first locomotive to carry passengers on rails
questions.explanation: Watt's separate condenser saved huge amounts of fuel, and his later rotary engines could turn machinery, so factories no longer had to be beside rivers. The tempting option describes Thomas Newcomen, whose engine pumped water from mines from 1712. Steam locomotives came later, with engineers such as Trevithick and Stephenson.

questions.stem: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830 with George Stephenson as engineer, is significant because it was:
options: the first inter-city railway using only steam locomotives
the first railway in which horses pulled wagons on rails
the first underground railway built under a city
the first railway line laid across the continent of North America
questions.explanation: Stephenson's Rocket won the trials to choose its engines, and the line carried passengers and goods between two industrial cities to a timetable. Horse-drawn wagonways on rails had existed for centuries, and London's first underground railway opened in 1863. Railways cut transport costs and helped spread industrialisation.

questions.stem: What did Britain's Factory Act of 1833 do?
options: Banned children under nine from working in textile mills
Banned all child labour in every industry in Britain completely
Set a minimum weekly wage for every factory worker
Gave factory workers the right to vote in elections
questions.explanation: The Act banned children under nine from textile factories, limited the hours of older children and appointed inspectors to enforce it. It was a first step, not an end to child labour: children kept working in many industries for decades. The 1847 Ten Hours Act later limited women and young people to ten hours a day.

questions.stem: The Mines Act of 1842 followed a report with shocking evidence about conditions underground. What did it do?
options: Closed every coal mine in England that employed children
Gave all miners an eight-hour working day with no loss of pay
Allowed children to work underground only during the night
Banned women, girls and boys under ten from working underground
questions.explanation: A royal commission described young children working alone in the dark as 'trappers' and women and girls hauling coal tubs, which outraged the public. The Act did not close mines or shorten men's hours; it removed women and young children from underground work.

questions.stem: The Luddites who broke machinery in parts of England between 1811 and 1816 were mainly:
options: coal miners striking for shorter hours underground
skilled textile workers losing jobs and wages to machines
farm labourers who wanted the right to vote in elections
factory owners destroying the machines of their rivals
questions.explanation: Stocking knitters and croppers in the Midlands and the North smashed frames and machines they blamed for low wages and unemployment; the government responded with troops and made machine-breaking a capital crime. Farm labourers rioted in the separate 'Swing' riots of 1830.

questions.stem: In 1834 six farm labourers from Tolpuddle in Dorset were sentenced to transportation to Australia. What had they done?
options: Formed a union and sworn a secret oath
Smashed machines in a cotton mill
Stolen sheep from their employer
Led a riot demanding the vote
questions.explanation: The 'Tolpuddle Martyrs' were convicted under an old law against secret oaths after forming a society to resist wage cuts. Mass protests and petitions won them pardons in 1836, and they became symbols of the right to form trade unions.

questions.stem: In 1854 Dr John Snow traced a London cholera outbreak to a public water pump in Broad Street. What did his work show?
options: Cholera was carried by rats and their fleas
Cholera spread through dirty water
Cholera spread through foul-smelling air
Cholera could be prevented by a vaccine
questions.explanation: Snow mapped the deaths and found they clustered around one pump, and persuaded officials to remove its handle. Most people at the time believed in 'miasma', the idea that disease came from bad air, which is why that option is tempting. His work supported public health reforms such as clean water supplies and sewers.

questions.stem: In the British Agricultural Revolution, the four-field rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover improved farming because:
options: fodder crops fed livestock and no field had to lie fallow
it let farmers grow wheat on every field every single year
steam tractors replaced the horses that pulled the ploughs
it shared the land out equally among all the village families
questions.explanation: Clover restored nitrogen to the soil and turnips fed animals through winter, so more livestock and more grain could be produced without leaving a field empty for a year. Steam tractors came much later, and enclosure actually concentrated land in fewer hands, pushing many rural workers towards the growing towns.

questions.stem: In the transatlantic 'triangular trade', what was carried on the Middle Passage?
options: Guns, cloth and other goods shipped from Europe to West Africa
Convicts shipped from Britain to the Australian penal colonies
Enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic to the Americas
Sugar, cotton and tobacco shipped from the Americas to Europe
questions.explanation: The Middle Passage was the middle leg of the triangle, in which enslaved people were packed into ships in brutal conditions, and many died on the voyage. The other two legs carried manufactured goods to Africa and plantation crops such as sugar back to Europe. Around 12 million Africans were forced onto ships over the course of the trade.

questions.stem: Which pair of British laws ended first the slave trade and then slavery itself in most of the British Empire?
options: The Slave Trade Act 1807 and the Slavery Abolition Act 1833
The Slavery Abolition Act 1807 and the Slave Trade Act 1833
The Reform Act 1832 and the Factory Act 1833
The Slave Trade Act 1772 and the Emancipation Act 1865
questions.explanation: Campaigners such as William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson first won the ban on Britain's trade in enslaved people in 1807, but slavery continued in British colonies until the 1833 Act. The swapped option is the common mix-up: trade first, slavery itself later. Slaveholders, not the enslaved, were paid compensation.

questions.stem: Olaudah Equiano helped the abolition movement in Britain mainly by:
options: introducing the abolition bill in Parliament
signing the Emancipation Proclamation
writing a bestselling account of his own enslavement
leading a successful slave revolt in Haiti
questions.explanation: Equiano's autobiography, published in 1789, described his capture, the Middle Passage and life as an enslaved man, giving the British public a first-hand African voice. William Wilberforce led the campaign in Parliament, Toussaint Louverture led the Haitian Revolution, and Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in the United States.

questions.stem: The Irish Famine of 1845–52 led to mass emigration. What was its immediate cause?
options: Blight that destroyed the potato crop
A war that burned farms across Ireland
A drought that dried up Ireland's rivers
Cholera brought in by ships from America
questions.explanation: A fungus-like disease rotted the potatoes that millions of poor families depended on. About a million people died and more than a million emigrated, to the United States, Canada, Britain and Australia. Food continued to be exported from Ireland during the famine, which is why many historians stress the role of British policy as well as the blight.

questions.stem: An Irish family emigrates to Victoria in 1853. Which pair of 'push' and 'pull' factors is correctly labelled?
options: Push: assisted passages to Victoria; pull: evictions in Ireland
Push: high wages in Victoria; pull: hunger at home in Ireland
Push: poverty after the Famine; pull: gold and jobs in Victoria
Push: gold and jobs in Victoria; pull: poverty after the Famine
questions.explanation: Push factors drive people away from home, such as hunger, eviction and poverty in post-Famine Ireland. Pull factors attract them to a destination, such as gold, jobs, high wages and assisted passages in Victoria. The other options all reverse the labels.

questions.stem: Mary Reibey, transported to NSW in 1792 for horse stealing at about thirteen, became a wealthy Sydney businesswoman. She is an example of:
options: a convict who remained in prison for her whole life
an emancipist who prospered after serving her sentence
an 'exclusive' who refused to mix socially with former convicts
a free settler who came out on an assisted passage
questions.explanation: Emancipists were convicts who had served their time or been pardoned, and some, such as Reibey and the architect Francis Greenway, became successful and respected. 'Exclusives' were free settlers and officials who looked down on emancipists. Reibey later appeared on the Australian $20 note.

questions.stem: Caroline Chisholm is remembered in colonial Australian history for:
options: helping single women and families migrate and find work
leading the nurses in the Crimean War hospitals
discovering payable gold near Bathurst in 1851
governing the colony of Van Diemen's Land
questions.explanation: From 1841 Chisholm ran a home for female immigrants in Sydney, found jobs for thousands of newcomers and later set up the Family Colonization Loan Society to help families pay their passage. Leading Crimean War nurses describes Florence Nightingale, and the 1851 gold find is credited to Edward Hargraves and his companions.

questions.stem: About how many convicts were transported to the Australian colonies between 1788 and 1868?
options: About 60,000
About 162,000
About 16,000
About 1.6 million
questions.explanation: Roughly 162,000 convicts were sent to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land, Moreton Bay, Norfolk Island and Western Australia. About one in seven was a woman. By comparison, around 12 million Africans were transported across the Atlantic in the slave trade.

questions.stem: The People's Charter of 1838 in Britain demanded reforms such as:
options: votes for all men, a secret ballot and payment of MPs
votes for women on equal terms and the abolition of the monarchy
an end to the slave trade and to child labour
free state schools and an eight-hour working day
questions.explanation: The Charter's six points were votes for all men, the secret ballot, payment of MPs, no property qualification for MPs, equal electorates and yearly elections. Chartists brought these ideas to the Australian colonies, and several, including the secret ballot in 1856, became law here well before they did in Britain.

questions.stem: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith argued that:
options: governments should own and run all major industry
trade should be restricted to protect home industry
workers should seize the factories by revolution
free markets and competition create wealth best
questions.explanation: Smith argued that individuals pursuing their own interest in competitive markets are guided, as if by an 'invisible hand', to benefit society, and he criticised restrictions on trade. These ideas became the basis of capitalism and free trade. Workers seizing factories is the revolutionary socialism of Marx and Engels.

questions.stem: In The Communist Manifesto (1848), Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels argued that:
options: the fittest individuals and nations rightly rise to rule the rest
workers should win their rights mainly by voting for liberal parties
history is a class struggle that workers would win by revolution
the market's 'invisible hand' works best when left completely alone
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels saw history as conflict between classes and predicted that the industrial working class would overthrow capitalism and create a society without private ownership of industry. The 'invisible hand' is Adam Smith's idea, and 'survival of the fittest' applied to societies is Social Darwinism.

questions.stem: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) caused controversy mainly because it:
options: proved that the Earth was only about six thousand years old
explained species changing by natural selection over vast time
claimed that humans were directly descended from modern chimpanzees
argued that some races were meant to rule over all the others
questions.explanation: Darwin argued that species are not fixed but change through natural selection, which challenged the literal reading of Genesis held by many Christians. He never said humans came from modern chimpanzees; humans and apes share ancestors. Using evolution to rank races was Social Darwinism, developed by others.

questions.stem: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), led at first by Toussaint Louverture, is significant because:
options: Haiti became a British colony at the end of the fighting
formerly enslaved people founded their own independent nation
it was the first colony anywhere in the Americas to win its independence
France freely granted Haiti independence by a peace treaty
questions.explanation: Enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, defeated French, Spanish and British forces, and in 1804 declared the independent state of Haiti. The United States had won independence earlier, in 1783, so Haiti was the second. France recognised Haiti only in 1825, after forcing it to pay a huge indemnity.

questions.stem: During the American Civil War, Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared that:
options: all African American men could vote in the next election
the Southern states could leave the Union in peace
enslaved people in the rebelling Confederate states were free
slavery was abolished throughout the whole of the United States
questions.explanation: The Proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion against the Union, and it allowed formerly enslaved men to join the Union army. Slavery was abolished across the whole country by the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, which is why the 'throughout the United States' option is tempting but wrong.

questions.stem: Emmeline Pankhurst's Women's Social and Political Union, founded in 1903, became known for:
options: peaceful petitions only, rejecting any law-breaking
campaigning to keep women out of factory work
winning the vote for British women in 1893
militant protest such as smashing windows to win the vote
questions.explanation: The WSPU's members, the suffragettes, used direct action including window-smashing, arson and hunger strikes. Peaceful campaigning describes the separate suffragists led by Millicent Fawcett. New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893; British women over 30 won it in 1918 and on equal terms with men in 1928.

questions.stem: Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891) influenced many Catholic workers, including in Australia. What position did it take?
options: Private property should be abolished and shared out equally by the state
Employers alone should decide wages, without any interference from the state or unions
Catholics should not join any trade union or workers' organisation
Workers deserved a just wage and could form unions, but socialism was rejected
questions.explanation: Rerum Novarum defended private property and opposed socialism, but said workers were owed a wage enough to live on and had the right to join associations such as unions. It encouraged many Catholics in Australia to support the labour movement and the idea of a fair 'living wage'.

questions.stem: At Munich in September 1938, Britain and France agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia. What is this policy of giving in to demands to avoid war called?
options: Isolationism
Containment
Conscription
Appeasement
questions.explanation: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain hoped that meeting Hitler's demands would satisfy him and keep the peace. Isolationism was the American policy of staying out of European affairs, and containment was the later Cold War policy of stopping the spread of communism. Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, showing appeasement had failed.

questions.stem: Why did the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939 make war in Europe more likely?
options: Hitler could invade Poland without fear of a Soviet attack
It made the Soviet Union join Britain and France against Germany
It returned Germany's lost colonies in Africa to German rule
It forced Italy to give up its alliance with Nazi Germany
questions.explanation: The two dictators agreed not to fight each other and secretly planned to divide Poland and Eastern Europe between them. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war two days later. The Soviet Union joined the Allies only after Germany invaded it in June 1941.

questions.stem: Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931) and Italy's invasion of Abyssinia (1935) both exposed which weakness of the League of Nations?
options: The United States used its veto to protect both nations
It had no army and could not stop powerful aggressors
It had voted to approve both invasions in advance
Japan and Italy had never been members of the League
questions.explanation: The League condemned both invasions, but without an army it could only use weak sanctions, and Japan and Italy simply left the League. Both had been members, and the United States never joined, so it held no veto. These failures encouraged further aggression in the late 1930s.

questions.stem: On 3 September 1939 Prime Minister Robert Menzies told Australians in a radio broadcast that, because Britain had declared war on Germany:
options: Australia would defend only Asia
Australia was also at war
Australia would stay neutral
Australia would await the US
questions.explanation: Menzies said it was his 'melancholy duty' to announce that, as a result of Britain's declaration, Australia was also at war. This reflected the view at the time that the British Empire went to war as one. The United States did not enter the war until December 1941.

questions.stem: In December 1941 Prime Minister John Curtin wrote that 'Australia looks to America'. What did he mean?
options: Australia would rely on the US, not Britain, for its defence
Australia would send all its troops to fight in North America
Australia would leave the British Commonwealth of Nations
Australia would adopt the American system of government
questions.explanation: With Japan advancing and Britain fighting for survival in Europe, Curtin signalled that Australia would turn to the United States as its main protector in the Pacific. Australia stayed in the Commonwealth and kept its system of government. The shift was confirmed when US forces under General MacArthur were based in Australia from 1942.

questions.stem: Why was the fall of Singapore on 15 February 1942 a shock for Australia?
options: The United States Pacific Fleet was destroyed in its harbour
Britain's main Pacific base was lost and about 15,000 Australians were captured
Japanese troops landed on the Australian mainland near Darwin the very next day
It was the first battle that Australian soldiers had ever lost
questions.explanation: Australians had been told that the Singapore naval base would protect them, so its surrender destroyed faith in British protection. Most of the Australians of the 8th Division became prisoners of war. Japan never invaded the Australian mainland, and the US Pacific Fleet had been attacked at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii.

questions.stem: On 19 February 1942, what happened in Darwin?
options: Japanese troops landed and captured the town
Allied forces surrendered the town to Japan
Japanese midget submarines entered the harbour
Japanese aircraft bombed the town and harbour
questions.explanation: Hundreds of Japanese aircraft attacked Darwin, sinking ships and killing more than 230 people; it was the first of many raids on northern Australia. Darwin was never captured. Midget submarines attacked Sydney Harbour in May–June 1942, which is a different event.

questions.stem: Australian prisoners of war on the Thai–Burma Railway, including at Hellfire Pass, suffered terribly because:
options: Japan forced them to build it by hand with little food or medicine
they were made to fight for Japan against British and Indian troops
they were held in German camps where Red Cross parcels were banned
they were marched along the Kokoda Track to New Guinea's north coast
questions.explanation: About 13,000 Australians were among the prisoners forced to cut the railway through jungle and rock in 1942–43, and thousands died of starvation, disease and brutal treatment. Surgeons such as Edward 'Weary' Dunlop became famous for caring for the sick. Kokoda was a battlefield in Papua, not a prisoner-of-war route.

questions.stem: Of more than 2,000 Australian and British prisoners of war held at Sandakan in Borneo, only six Australians survived. What caused the deaths?
options: The sinking of the prison ship that was carrying them to Japan
A mass escape that was put down by the camp guards
Starvation, disease, killings and forced death marches
Allied bombing raids that destroyed the prison camp
questions.explanation: In 1945 the Japanese forced the weakened prisoners on marches through the jungle to Ranau, and those who could not go on were killed or left to die; the six survivors had escaped. The sinking of a prison ship describes a different tragedy, the Montevideo Maru in 1942, and the mass escape option describes the Cowra breakout of Japanese prisoners.

questions.stem: In August 1944 more than a thousand Japanese prisoners of war tried to break out of a camp in New South Wales. Where was it?
options: Tatura
Hay
Cowra
Changi
questions.explanation: Hundreds of Japanese prisoners died in the Cowra breakout, along with four Australian soldiers, and those who got out were recaptured within days. Tatura in Victoria and Hay in NSW held civilian internees and prisoners but had no such breakout, while Changi was the Japanese-run camp in Singapore where Allied prisoners were held.

questions.stem: Under the National Security Act 1939, the Australian government interned thousands of people during World War II. Who were they mainly?
options: British migrants who had arrived after 1930
Residents of German, Italian and Japanese background
Soldiers who refused to serve outside Australia
Aboriginal men who had tried to enlist in the army
questions.explanation: People from 'enemy' nations, including many who had lived in Australia for years or were naturalised, were held in camps such as Tatura, Loveday and Hay. Some were Jewish refugees from Nazism, such as the 'Dunera boys' sent from Britain in 1940. The same Act allowed censorship, rationing and control of workers.

questions.stem: Why did the Australian government introduce ration books for goods such as tea, sugar, butter and clothing from 1942?
options: To punish families who had refused to buy government war bonds
Because Australian farmers had stopped growing any food
To stop prices falling too low once the war had ended
To share scarce goods fairly and free resources for the war
questions.explanation: Rationing meant each person could buy only a set amount using coupons, so shortages caused by the war, shipping losses and supplies to troops were shared fairly. Farmers kept producing, but much food went to the armed forces and to Britain. Some rationing continued until 1950.

questions.stem: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, Allied forces:
options: landed on the beaches of Normandy in northern France
evacuated their armies from the beaches at Dunkirk
captured Berlin and ended the war in Europe
dropped the first atomic bomb on Japan
questions.explanation: Operation Overlord opened a second front in Western Europe, and about 3,000 Australians took part, mostly in the air force and navy. The Dunkirk evacuation was in 1940, Soviet forces captured Berlin in May 1945, and the atomic bombs were dropped in August 1945.

questions.stem: What was new about the Nuremberg trials of 1945–46?
options: They were the first criminal trials of any kind to be held anywhere in Germany
Only ordinary soldiers were tried, while the leaders went free
The accused were judged by juries of ordinary German citizens
National leaders were held personally responsible for crimes against humanity
questions.explanation: An international tribunal tried leading Nazis for crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity, rejecting the defence that they were only following orders or the laws of their state. The idea led to later international law, including the 1948 Genocide Convention. The judges came from the four Allied powers, not German juries.

questions.stem: The word 'genocide', used in the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, was coined in 1944 by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin. What does it describe?
options: Any killing of civilians by soldiers or aircraft in the course of a war
The forced movement of refugees across national borders
The use of nuclear weapons against cities and civilians
Acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
questions.explanation: Lemkin, a Polish Jewish lawyer, combined the Greek genos (people or race) and the Latin -cide (killing) to describe the Holocaust and earlier atrocities. Genocide is defined by intent to destroy a group, which is narrower than all civilian deaths in war. Australia was among the early countries to ratify the Convention, in 1949.

questions.stem: The 'Brisbane Line' was a controversial claim made during World War II. What was it?
options: That a railway was being built to carry troops from Brisbane to Darwin
That plans existed to defend only the south-east if Japan invaded
That Japanese troops had landed on the coast north of Brisbane
That Brisbane had become the base of the British Pacific Fleet
questions.explanation: In 1942 the Labor minister Eddie Ward claimed the previous government had planned to abandon northern Australia and defend only the area south of a line near Brisbane. Historians have found no evidence of an adopted plan of that kind, which is why it is called a controversy rather than a policy. Japan never landed troops on the Australian mainland.

questions.stem: Until 1966, a woman with a permanent job in the Commonwealth Public Service:
options: had to resign her permanent job when she married
was paid more than a man doing the same work
could work only in wartime munitions factories
was required to retire at the age of forty
questions.explanation: This rule was called the 'marriage bar'; married women could work only as temporary staff, losing pay, superannuation and promotion. It reflected the belief that a married woman's place was in the home. Campaigners including Merle Thornton helped end it in 1966.

questions.stem: In 1965 Merle Thornton and Rosalie Bogner chained themselves to the bar of Brisbane's Regatta Hotel. What were they protesting?
options: The low wages paid to women working as barmaids
The marriage bar in the Commonwealth Public Service
A law stopping women from entering Parliament House
A rule barring women from drinking in public bars
questions.explanation: Women were not allowed to drink in the public bar and were sent to a separate lounge, so the protest was a deliberate and very visible challenge to everyday discrimination. Thornton did also campaign against the marriage bar, but that was not what this protest targeted.

questions.stem: How did the 1972 equal pay decision go further than the 1969 decision?
options: It applied 'equal pay for work of equal value'
It gave women the vote in federal elections
It set women's wages at 75% of men's wages
It ended all pay for married women in jobs
questions.explanation: The 1969 decision covered only women doing the same work as men, which left most women, who worked in 'female' jobs, unaffected. The 1972 decision extended equal pay to work of equal value. Setting women's wages at 75% of men's was the 1950 basic wage decision, an earlier stage, and women had the federal vote from 1902.

questions.stem: Germaine Greer's book The Female Eunuch (1970) is closely linked with which movement?
options: The anti-conscription movement
Women's Liberation
The suffrage movement
Temperance
questions.explanation: The book argued that women had been taught to accept limited roles, and it became a key text of Women's Liberation, or second-wave feminism. The suffrage movement for the vote came earlier, in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Temperance campaigned against alcohol.

questions.stem: The Women's Electoral Lobby, formed in 1972, became known for which tactic?
options: Standing its own candidates for every seat in the federal Parliament
Running as a branch of the Labor Party that only women could join
Calling general strikes of women workers to close down factories
Surveying candidates on women's issues and publishing their answers
questions.explanation: Before the 1972 federal election WEL questioned candidates on issues such as equal pay, childcare and abortion and published their answers and ratings, so voters could judge them. It was independent of the political parties. In 1973 the new Whitlam government appointed Elizabeth Reid as the Prime Minister's adviser on women's affairs.

questions.stem: What did the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 make unlawful?
options: Refusing to rent a home or sell a house to someone because of their race
Unfair treatment at work or in services because of sex or marriage
Paying any worker less than the federal minimum wage
Dismissing workers because they had joined a trade union
questions.explanation: The Act covered areas such as employment, education and access to goods and services, and also addressed sexual harassment. It relied on Australia's ratification in 1983 of the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW). Discrimination on the grounds of race had already been made unlawful by the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.

questions.stem: Which two women were the first elected to the federal Parliament, in 1943?
options: Edith Cowan and Vida Goldstein
Julia Gillard and Quentin Bryce
Joan Kirner and Carmen Lawrence
Enid Lyons and Dorothy Tangney
questions.explanation: Enid Lyons won a seat in the House of Representatives and Dorothy Tangney a Senate seat, more than forty years after women won the right to stand. Edith Cowan was elected to the Western Australian Parliament in 1921, and Joan Kirner and Carmen Lawrence became the first female state premiers in 1990.

questions.stem: Put these milestones in order. Which came first?
options: Julia Gillard becomes Prime Minister
Edith Cowan elected to a state parliament
Enid Lyons elected to federal Parliament
Carmen Lawrence becomes a state premier
questions.explanation: Edith Cowan entered the Western Australian Parliament in 1921, Enid Lyons the House of Representatives in 1943, Carmen Lawrence became Premier of Western Australia in 1990, and Julia Gillard became Prime Minister in 2010. In 2008 Quentin Bryce became the first female Governor-General.

questions.stem: Which country was the first self-governing nation to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
options: Australia
Britain
The United States
New Zealand
questions.explanation: New Zealand women won the vote in 1893 after petitions organised by Kate Sheppard. The Commonwealth of Australia followed in 1902, Britain partly in 1918 and fully in 1928, and the United States in 1920 with the 19th Amendment.

questions.stem: In 1945 Australia's population was about 7.4 million. Which best describes where most Australians' families came from?
options: Asia
The Pacific Islands
Britain and Ireland
Southern Europe
questions.explanation: Decades of the White Australia policy and British migration meant the population was overwhelmingly of British and Irish origin, apart from First Nations peoples. Large-scale migration from southern Europe began only after the war, and Asian migration grew after the policy was dismantled.

questions.stem: From 1947 Immigration Minister Arthur Calwell arranged for which group to be brought to Australia from camps in Europe?
options: Displaced persons left homeless by the war
Asian students under the Colombo Plan
Refugees escaping the Vietnam War
Chinese miners bound for the goldfields
questions.explanation: More than 170,000 displaced persons, many from the Baltic states, Poland and Yugoslavia, came between 1947 and the early 1950s, usually agreeing to work for two years where the government sent them. The Colombo Plan began in 1950 and the Vietnamese refugees came after 1975.

questions.stem: Why were British migrants on the post-war assisted passage scheme called 'Ten Pound Poms'?
options: Each family received ten pounds a week from the government on arrival
Each migrant had to show ten pounds in savings before being allowed to land
Migrants were paid ten pounds to work for a year on the Snowy Scheme
Adults paid only ten pounds and the government paid the rest of the fare
questions.explanation: The scheme, which began in 1947, made the long voyage cheap so as to attract British migrants, in line with the aim of keeping Australia mainly British. Children often travelled free. Over the following decades more than a million Britons came this way.

questions.stem: What was Bonegilla, near Albury–Wodonga, from 1947 to 1971?
options: An institution for Aboriginal children removed from their families
A reception and training centre for newly arrived migrants
A detention centre for asylum seekers who arrived by boat
A prisoner-of-war camp for captured Japanese soldiers
questions.explanation: More than 300,000 migrants, many from non-English-speaking European countries, passed through this former army camp, where they learned English and were sent on to jobs. Mandatory detention of asylum seekers began in 1992, long after Bonegilla closed.

questions.stem: How did the Colombo Plan, which began in 1950, help change Australian attitudes to Asia?
options: It abolished the White Australia policy in a single law
Thousands of Asian students studied at Australian universities
It allowed unlimited migration from Asian countries from 1950
It sent Australian troops to defend the city of Colombo
questions.explanation: Under the Plan, Australia gave aid to South and South-East Asian countries and brought students to study here, creating personal and diplomatic links while the White Australia policy still limited migration. The policy was not abolished until 1973.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the White Australia policy ended?
options: It ended when the six colonies federated as Australia in 1901
It was eased under Holt in 1966 and formally ended by Whitlam in 1973
It was abolished in one law passed by the first Menzies government in 1949
It ended automatically when the 1967 referendum was approved
questions.explanation: The policy was dismantled in stages: the Holt government allowed more non-European migrants with skills in 1966, and the Whitlam government removed race as a factor in 1973, followed by the Racial Discrimination Act 1975. The 1967 referendum was about Aboriginal people and the Constitution, not immigration, and Federation in 1901 was when the policy began.

questions.stem: After the fall of Saigon in 1975, how did the Fraser government respond to refugees from Vietnam?
options: It sent all boat arrivals to processing camps on Nauru and Manus
It returned every boat that reached northern Australia straight to Vietnam
It resettled tens of thousands, many from camps in South-East Asia
It refused to accept any refugees at all from Asian countries
questions.explanation: Small boats began arriving in northern Australia from 1976, and the government chose to resettle large numbers of Indochinese refugees through an organised program, with bipartisan support. Offshore processing on Nauru and Manus Island came much later, under the 2001 'Pacific Solution'.

questions.stem: From the 1970s, which policy replaced assimilation, encouraging migrants to keep their languages and cultures while sharing Australian values and laws?
options: Multiculturalism
Protectionism
Federalism
Isolationism
questions.explanation: Immigration Minister Al Grassby promoted 'a multicultural society' in 1973, and the Fraser government's Galbally Report of 1978 led to services such as SBS. Assimilation had expected migrants to give up their own cultures and blend in.

questions.stem: Which policy, introduced after the Tampa affair in 2001, sent asylum seekers arriving by boat to processing centres outside Australia?
options: The Pacific Solution, with centres on Nauru and Manus Island
The Colombo Plan, with processing centres in Sri Lanka
Mandatory detention, first introduced by the Whitlam government
The White Australia policy, brought back by a 2001 law
questions.explanation: When the Norwegian ship Tampa rescued asylum seekers in August 2001, the Howard government refused to let them land and set up offshore processing. Mandatory detention of unauthorised arrivals in Australia had begun earlier, in 1992 under the Keating government.

questions.stem: The Bringing Them Home report (1997) was the result of a national inquiry into:
options: the separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander deaths in police cells, prisons and juvenile detention
native title claims made after the High Court's Mabo decision
the effects of the 1967 referendum on Aboriginal voting rights
questions.explanation: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission heard evidence from hundreds of people and found that thousands of children had been forcibly removed. It recommended an apology and reparations. Deaths in custody were examined by a separate Royal Commission (1987–91), which is the usual mix-up.

questions.stem: On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd:
options: apologised in Parliament to the Stolen Generations
signed a national treaty with First Nations peoples
presented the Uluru Statement from the Heart
announced the High Court's Mabo decision
questions.explanation: The National Apology was moved as the first business of the new Parliament and watched by crowds across the country. No national treaty has been signed. The Uluru Statement was issued by First Nations delegates in 2017, and the Mabo decision was made by the High Court in 1992.

questions.stem: The 1965 Freedom Ride through NSW country towns, organised by University of Sydney students in Student Action for Aborigines, took its name and tactics from:
options: Gandhi's Salt March against British rule in India
the 1938 Day of Mourning protest held in Sydney
the Gurindji walk-off from Wave Hill station
the 1961 Freedom Rides through the southern United States
questions.explanation: Black and white American activists had ridden interstate buses in 1961 to challenge segregation, and the Australian students copied the idea to expose segregation at places such as the Moree swimming pool and the Walgett RSL. The Wave Hill walk-off began in 1966, after the Freedom Ride.

questions.stem: Rosa Parks's arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955 led to:
options: a year-long boycott of the city's segregated buses
the immediate end of segregation across the US
the assassination of Martin Luther King
the first Freedom Ride through the southern states
questions.explanation: Parks refused to give up her seat to a white passenger, and Black residents, led by a young Martin Luther King, boycotted the buses for over a year until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unlawful. Segregation elsewhere continued until the civil rights laws of the 1960s, and King was assassinated in 1968.

questions.stem: Paul Keating's Redfern Speech in December 1992 is remembered because he:
options: declared an end to the policy of removing Aboriginal children
acknowledged that non-Indigenous Australians had caused the dispossession
delivered a formal national apology to the Stolen Generations in Parliament
announced that the High Court had restored terra nullius
questions.explanation: Speaking to launch the International Year of the World's Indigenous People, Keating said that 'we' took the land, brought the diseases and took the children, an unusually direct admission by a Prime Minister. The formal national apology came from Kevin Rudd in 2008, and the Mabo decision earlier in 1992 had rejected terra nullius.

questions.stem: In the Wik decision of 1996, the High Court found that:
options: pastoral leases always extinguished native title
the Wik peoples owned all of Cape York as freehold
pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title
native title had never existed in Australian law
questions.explanation: The Wik and Thayorre peoples of Cape York showed that native title could exist alongside a pastoral lease, though where the two conflicted the lease would prevail. The decision alarmed pastoralists, and the Howard government responded with the 'Ten Point Plan' amendments in 1998.

questions.stem: What did the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017) call for?
options: A First Nations Voice in the Constitution and a Makarrata Commission
Aboriginal people to be counted in the national census
A separate Aboriginal state to be created in central and northern Australia
All Crown land to be returned to Traditional Owners at once
questions.explanation: Delegates at the First Nations National Constitutional Convention asked for a Voice to Parliament protected by the Constitution and a Makarrata Commission for agreement-making and truth-telling. Counting Aboriginal people in the census was part of the 1967 referendum. A referendum on the Voice in 2023 did not pass.

questions.stem: In 1971 large protests met the touring South African rugby team, the Springboks, in Australian cities. What was the main reason?
options: South Africa had banned Australians from entering the country
The tour was held during a national rugby players' strike
South Africa's apartheid system chose sporting teams by race
The team had refused to play against any Australian state sides
questions.explanation: Under apartheid, South Africa enforced racial segregation in every part of life, including sport. Protesters saw the tour as support for racism, and Australian activists linked apartheid with discrimination against First Nations people at home. International boycotts helped isolate South Africa until apartheid ended in the early 1990s.

questions.stem: The NSW Aboriginal Languages Act 2017 is significant because it:
options: recognised Aboriginal languages and set out to revive and protect them
made learning an Aboriginal language compulsory in every NSW school from Year 7
declared English the only official language of New South Wales
banned schools from teaching Aboriginal languages to children
questions.explanation: The Act acknowledged that past laws and policies had damaged Aboriginal languages and committed the state to supporting their reclaiming, revitalisation and growth. Language revival programs are part of a wider reclaiming of Cultures and identities. Earlier policies on missions and reserves had often banned Aboriginal people from speaking their languages.

questions.stem: Rachel Carson's book Silent Spring (1962) warned about:
options: the hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica
rising sea levels caused by global warming
radiation leaking from nuclear power plants
the harm pesticides such as DDT did to wildlife
questions.explanation: Carson showed how pesticides built up in food chains and killed birds and other wildlife, and her book helped launch the modern environmental movement. The ozone hole was reported in 1985, and climate change became a major public issue later in the century.

questions.stem: The campaign to save Lake Pedder in south-west Tasmania in the early 1970s led to:
options: the founding of the world's first green political party
the dam being abandoned and the lake fully protected
the High Court's ruling in the Tasmanian Dam Case
Greenpeace being founded in Hobart to fight the dam
questions.explanation: Campaigners formed the United Tasmania Group in 1972 to contest the state election, the first green party in the world. The campaign failed and the lake was flooded for hydro-electricity in 1972, which is why the 'abandoned' option is wrong. The Tasmanian Dam Case concerned the Franklin River in 1983.

questions.stem: In the early 1970s Jack Mundey and the Builders Labourers Federation imposed 'green bans' in Sydney. What were they?
options: Heavy fines on factories that polluted Sydney Harbour
Union refusals to work on sites that residents wanted to save
Laws stopping private cars from entering the city centre
Bans on selling drinks in non-recyclable containers
questions.explanation: The first green ban, in 1971, protected Kelly's Bush in Hunters Hill at the request of local women, and later bans helped save historic parts of The Rocks and Centennial Park from development. They were an unusual alliance between a trade union and residents' groups.

questions.stem: In the Tasmanian Dam Case (1983), on what basis did the High Court rule that the Commonwealth could stop the Franklin Dam?
options: Its external affairs power let it carry out the World Heritage Convention
The Constitution gives the Commonwealth control of every river in Australia
Tasmanian voters had rejected the dam in a statewide referendum
The dam site was on Commonwealth defence land, not state land
questions.explanation: Because the area was World Heritage listed and Australia had signed the 1972 World Heritage Convention, the Court held that Commonwealth laws protecting it were valid under the external affairs power. Tasmania's 1981 referendum offered voters only a choice between two dam sites, so it did not reject the dam.

questions.stem: In 1985 the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was bombed and sunk in Auckland Harbour. Who was responsible?
options: French secret service agents
The New Zealand Navy
Japanese whaling crews
United States marines
questions.explanation: The ship was preparing to protest against French nuclear tests at Mururoa Atoll, and a photographer on board was killed. New Zealand police arrested two French agents, and France eventually admitted responsibility. The attack strengthened anti-nuclear feeling across the Pacific.

questions.stem: Britain tested nuclear weapons at Maralinga in South Australia in the 1950s. Why are these tests a serious issue for First Nations Australians?
options: Anangu people were moved off Country and exposed to radioactive fallout
The test sites were on land that Aboriginal owners had sold to the British government
Aboriginal people were safely evacuated and compensated straight away
The tests were held only on uninhabited islands far out at sea
questions.explanation: Maralinga Tjarutja and other Anangu people were removed from their lands, and some were exposed to radiation; a Royal Commission in 1984–85 reported on the harm. The land was never sold, and compensation and clean-up came only decades later. Earlier British tests were held on the Monte Bello Islands, but Maralinga is on the mainland.

questions.stem: Why did the Chernobyl disaster of 1986 change attitudes to nuclear power around the world?
options: It was the first nuclear accident ever to have occurred
A reactor explosion spread radioactive fallout across Europe
A nuclear bomb was accidentally dropped on a Soviet city
It caused a tsunami that flooded the coast of Japan
questions.explanation: An explosion and fire at a reactor in Soviet Ukraine released radioactive material that spread over much of Europe, and a large area around the plant is still closed. There had been earlier accidents, such as Three Mile Island in the United States in 1979, and the tsunami option describes Fukushima in 2011.

questions.stem: What did the Montreal Protocol of 1987 do?
options: Set binding targets for cutting carbon dioxide emissions
Banned commercial whaling in all of the world's oceans
Created World Heritage listing for important natural sites
Phased out chemicals such as CFCs that damage the ozone layer
questions.explanation: The agreement phased out ozone-depleting chemicals used in aerosol sprays and refrigerators, and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering, which is why it is often called the most successful environmental treaty. Binding greenhouse gas targets came with the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which Australia ratified in 2007.

questions.stem: The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm is significant because it:
options: listed the Great Barrier Reef as a World Heritage site
was the first major UN conference on the environment and set up UNEP
set legally binding limits on carbon emissions for every member country
banned all nuclear weapons testing in the Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: The conference put the environment on the international agenda and created the UN Environment Programme. Binding emissions targets came later with Kyoto, and the Great Barrier Reef was World Heritage listed in 1981.

questions.stem: In 1998 the Mirarr Traditional Owners led a blockade at Jabiluka, inside Kakadu National Park. What were they opposing?
options: Sand mining on K'gari (Fraser Island)
Logging in the Daintree rainforest
A new uranium mine on their Country
A hydro-electric dam on the Franklin
questions.explanation: Led by Senior Traditional Owner Yvonne Margarula, the Mirarr campaigned with environmental groups against the mine, which was never developed; they later gained the right to veto future mining there. The other options are real campaigns in Tasmania and Queensland, but not Jabiluka.

questions.stem: In 1946 Winston Churchill said that an 'iron curtain' had come down across Europe. What did he mean?
options: Britain had built a defensive wall along its southern coastline
Germany had rebuilt its fortifications along the French border
The Berlin Wall had been built to divide the German capital
Europe was split between Soviet-controlled East and democratic West
questions.explanation: Churchill was describing how the Soviet Union had taken control of Eastern Europe after World War II, marking the start of the Cold War. The Berlin Wall was not built until 1961 and fell in 1989.

questions.stem: Why did Australia send forces to the Korean War (1950–53)?
options: To support the UN effort to stop communist North Korea taking the South
To defend South Korea, which had been an Australian-run territory since 1945
To help Japan regain control of its former colony of Korea
Because North Korean aircraft had attacked northern Australia
questions.explanation: The Menzies government saw the North Korean invasion as communist expansion that had to be resisted, and joined the United Nations force led by the United States. Australian battalions fought at battles such as Kapyong in 1951. Fear of communism in Asia, and the wish for an alliance with the US, shaped Australian policy.

questions.stem: In 1950 the Menzies government passed the Communist Party Dissolution Act. What happened next?
options: The Communist Party was banned in Australia until the 1990s
Voters approved a ban on the party at the 1951 referendum
Communist Party members were sent to fight in Korea
The High Court struck it down and a 1951 referendum to allow it failed
questions.explanation: In 1951 the High Court ruled the Act invalid, and Menzies then asked voters to give the Commonwealth the power to ban the party. The referendum narrowly failed, after Labor leader H.V. Evatt campaigned against it as a threat to civil liberties.

questions.stem: In 1954 Vladimir Petrov, an officer at the Soviet embassy in Canberra, defected to Australia. Why did this matter?
options: It led Australia to end all trade and diplomatic ties with Britain for a decade
It revealed that the Prime Minister had been a Soviet agent
It fed fears of Soviet spying and led to a Royal Commission on espionage
It caused Australia to send its first troops to the Korean War
questions.explanation: Petrov and his wife Evdokia brought documents about Soviet spying, and the affair, which broke just before the 1954 election, deepened fear of communism. Labor's leader Evatt claimed some documents were concocted to damage Labor, adding to the tensions that split the party in 1955. Australian troops had gone to Korea back in 1950.

questions.stem: The Labor split of 1955 led to the creation of the Democratic Labor Party (DLP). What mainly divided Labor?
options: Whether to end the White Australia policy straight away
How to fight communist influence in the trade unions
Whether to give women the vote in federal elections
Whether Australia should join the Second World War
questions.explanation: Anti-communist 'Industrial Groups' in the unions, many of them Catholic, clashed with Evatt and the party leadership, and the breakaway group became the DLP. Its preferences helped keep the Coalition in power for many years. Women had the federal vote from 1902, and the war had ended in 1945.

questions.stem: Which best describes Australia's 'long boom' of the 1950s and 1960s?
options: High unemployment and falling wages caused by the end of the war
A collapse in wool prices that closed most of Australia's factories
Rapid inflation caused by the oil shock and rising world prices
Low unemployment, rising home ownership and strong wool and mineral exports
questions.explanation: Under Menzies, protected manufacturing grew, migrants found work easily, more families owned homes and cars, and wool and later iron ore earned export income. The 1973 oil shock helped end the boom, so it came after this period.

questions.stem: Under the National Service scheme introduced in 1964, how were young men chosen, with some sent to Vietnam?
options: A ballot drew birth dates, and men born on those dates were called up
Every man who turned eighteen was called up automatically into the army
Only volunteers who answered newspaper advertisements were taken
Men were chosen according to their final school exam results
questions.explanation: Men had to register at age twenty, and marbles marked with birth dates were drawn in what was called the 'birthday ballot'. From 1965 national servicemen could be sent overseas, and around 15,000 served in Vietnam. Conscription was ended by the Whitlam government in December 1972.

questions.stem: In August 1966 Australian soldiers fought a major battle in a rubber plantation in Vietnam. What is it known as?
options: Long Tan
Kapyong
Kokoda
Tobruk
questions.explanation: At Long Tan, D Company of 6RAR, fewer than 110 men, held off a much larger Vietnamese force in heavy rain until help arrived. Kapyong was an Australian battle in the Korean War, while Kokoda and Tobruk were World War II battles.

questions.stem: The Vietnam Moratorium marches of 1970 were significant because:
options: they welcomed Australian troops home after victory in Vietnam
they were organised by the government to build support for the war
they forced the immediate end of conscription on the same day
huge crowds in Australian cities opposed the war and conscription
questions.explanation: Tens of thousands marched in Melbourne alone, showing how far opinion had shifted against the war since 1965. Conscription continued until the Whitlam government ended it in December 1972, and the last Australian troops left Vietnam without victory.

questions.stem: On 11 November 1975 Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed the Whitlam government. What had caused the crisis?
options: Whitlam had refused to call an election that was overdue
The Senate had blocked the government's budget (supply) bills
The government had lost a vote of confidence in the House of Representatives
The High Court had ruled that the government was illegal
questions.explanation: The Coalition-controlled Senate refused to pass supply, so the government was running out of money, and Kerr dismissed Whitlam and appointed Malcolm Fraser as caretaker Prime Minister. Whitlam still had the confidence of the House, which is why the Dismissal remains so controversial. Fraser won the election that followed.

questions.stem: The fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 is seen as a symbol of:
options: the founding of the United Nations in Berlin
the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe
the beginning of the Cold War in divided Europe
the reunification of North and South Korea
questions.explanation: East Germans crossed freely to the West for the first time since 1961, and communist governments across Eastern Europe fell within months; Germany reunified in 1990. The Cold War had begun in the late 1940s, and Korea remains divided.

questions.stem: Why did the Bali bombings of October 2002 have such a deep effect on Australia?
options: They were the first terrorist attacks in history
Australian troops were based in Bali at the time
They led Australia to declare war on Indonesia
88 of the 202 people killed were Australians
questions.explanation: The attacks on nightclubs in Kuta by the terrorist group Jemaah Islamiyah killed more Australians than any other single terrorist act. They came a year after the 11 September 2001 attacks in the United States, and Australia and Indonesia cooperated closely to catch those responsible.
